builder_plan.scenario: Your coding assistant makes changes that still need substantial repair before merging.
builder_plan.change: Try the technique on held-out issues from a repository with reliable tests.
builder_plan.baseline: The same coding agent, repository snapshot, tools, and token budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct patches, regression failures, human repair time, and total cost per accepted change.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood
summary: It replaces training a code localizer to mimic reference patch edits with supervised fine-tuning on a frozen fixer's likelihood of producing a verified patch, avoiding test execution and reinforcement learning. Costs are modest: roughly 1,629 test-verified teacher trajectories, a frozen fixer for scoring, and fine-tuning of a 4B model, which fits a single 24 GB GPU. It can fail because gains are small and noisy at this scale (8 vs. 6 solved), the method depends on verified teacher trajectories that may not exist for the reader's codebase, and 4B agents remain limited by time budgets, repetition loops, and edit quality regardless of localization improvements.
rationale: The pipeline is reproducible on constrained hardware and addresses a real bottleneck in small coding agents, but the modest and partially statistically fragile improvements, plus the need for domain-matched verified trajectories, justify a small-scale validation rather than direct production adoption.
technique: Fixer-guided code localization via weighted SFT

claims.statement: It replaces training a code localizer to mimic reference patch edits with supervised fine-tuning on a frozen fixer's likelihood of producing a verified patch, avoiding test execution and reinforcement learning. Costs are modest: roughly 1,629 test-verified teacher trajectories, a frozen fixer for scoring, and fine-tuning of a 4B model, which fits a single 24 GB GPU. It can fail because gains are small and noisy at this scale (8 vs. 6 solved), the method depends on verified teacher trajectories that may not exist for the reader's codebase, and 4B agents remain limited by time budgets, repetition loops, and edit quality regardless of localization improvements.

The localizer matches the teacher's bug-finding rate while using 27.5% less code; one EM round raises solved tasks from 6 to 8 of 78 on the dev set (up to 11 of 78 for a single trained agent versus 8 for the base model).
